Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Vignette:
The collision happened on a Tuesday afternoon when Kwame was driving home after a community performance. A delivery truck ran the red light, striking his passenger side with a force that folded the metal and threw him forward against the shoulder strap. He felt the impact shudder through his ribs, heard the glass shatter in a sharp, rolling wave, and saw the sky tilt as his seatbelt locked. For weeks after, he felt like he was only remembering parts of what happened, and the rest was missing. He could not tell a clear story of what happened even to himself, the sequence of events sitting side by side rather than in a line. When he tried to deliberately remember what happened, he found it difficult to access the memory, the details sliding back into place like loose tiles. Kwame was sixty-eight, widowed, and African, a man who had spent his adult life moving through the world with the practiced surety of a dancer. Now, he can no longer trust his own body. A sudden stiffness in his shoulders or a deep ache in his knees made him pause, his limbs feeling like separate, uncertain structures. He cannot trust that he will do the right thing, his judgments feeling unsteady the moment he is startled. These appraisals ran parallel to the slow, uncoordinated response that followed the crash. He was certain that when something takes longer than expected, something bad is happening. The tow truck arrived late, the paramedics seemed unprepared, and the hospital intake process dragged on. The people or institutions that should have protected him let me down, a phrase he had begun to use internally until it settled into his daily rhythm as a steady, unspoken warning. In the present, Kwame lives in a third-floor apartment and spends his mornings in the studio where he teaches movement classes. The wooden floors and mirrored walls give him a familiar anchor, yet the space constantly demands his attention. He feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall where he can see the room, his eyes tracking the door and the windows. When a student drops a yoga block or a chair scrapes abruptly against the floor, his breath catches. He is on high alert when he hears unexpected or loud sounds, his shoulders tightening as if bracing for another impact. He avoids going out after dusk, preferring the predictable quiet of his apartment. He also steers clear of seeing people that he socialised with before the event. Their familiar faces remind him of the life he had, and their questions about his health feel like tests he might fail, his mind holding the two states of being at once. In therapy, Kwame sits with his shoulders squared to the room, listening but carefully sidestepping certain topics. He avoids thinking about anything discussed in therapy, his attention drifting when the conversation demands too much of his focus. He watches the clock. If a dialogue lingers past its expected minute, he assumes something bad is unfolding. The studio mirrors catch his reflection as he demonstrates a gentle turn, but he moves with a deliberate caution, his body a separate entity he must command rather than inhabit. His PCL-5 score of 67 confirmed what he had been feeling, yet the number sat on the page, separate from the quiet withdrawals that had finally brought him to the therapist’s door. His sister had left a note about his unopened mail, and he realized he had stopped answering calls entirely. He is hoping to reclaim the ability to move without constantly calculating the distance to a wall or the timing of a sound. Most of all, he fears that his body will betray him again, and that the story of his survival will remain forever incomplete, suspended in the space between the shatter of glass and the slow approach of the tow truck.
